sections.content: Dayton, Ohio doesn't always grab headlines the way Phoenix or Tampa does, but investors who know where to look are quietly building serious wealth here. With median home prices well below the national average, a recovering local economy, and strong rental demand from a large workforce population, the opportunity to find profitable real estate deals in Dayton OH is very real in 2024. Whether you're brand new to investing or a seasoned wholesaler looking for your next market, this guide walks you through everything you need to know. If you're just getting started, check out the Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide first — it'll give you a solid foundation before diving into a specific market.
Dayton OH Market Overview: Why Investors Are Paying Attention

Dayton is the sixth-largest city in Ohio and sits in Montgomery County, about 55 miles north of Cincinnati. The metro area has a population of roughly 800,000 people. After decades of decline tied to manufacturing losses, Dayton has been reinventing itself around healthcare, aerospace, and defense industries. Wright-Patterson Air Force Base alone employs over 27,000 people, making it the largest single-site employer in Ohio. That stable, well-paying employment base is a major driver of rental demand and property value stability. The city also benefits from several major hospitals and the University of Dayton, which keeps a steady flow of renters in certain neighborhoods year-round.
Average Home Prices and Entry Points for Investors

One of the biggest draws for investors eyeing real estate deals in Dayton OH is the low cost of entry. As of 2024, the median home price in Dayton sits around $135,000 to $155,000, compared to the national median of over $400,000. Distressed properties — the kind that attract wholesalers and flippers — can often be acquired for $30,000 to $70,000 in many zip codes. After-repair values (ARVs) in desirable neighborhoods regularly hit $120,000 to $200,000, leaving room for solid profit margins. Best Neighborhoods in Dayton for Real Estate Investors

Not all Dayton zip codes are created equal. Knowing where to focus your deal-finding efforts can mean the difference between a profitable investment and a money pit. Here are the areas getting the most investor attention right now.
Top Neighborhoods to Target

items: Oakwood: One of Dayton's most desirable suburbs, with strong ARVs between $200,000 and $350,000. Great for higher-end flips where quality rehabs command top dollar.
Kettering: A stable, family-friendly suburb with consistent rental demand and resale values. Median prices hover around $150,000 to $180,000, making it ideal for buy-and-hold investors.
Beavercreek: Close to Wright-Patterson AFB, this area has low vacancy rates and strong tenant quality. Military families create reliable rental demand throughout the year.
Huber Heights: Affordable entry points with solid rental yields. Single-family homes here often cash flow well as long-term rentals or BRRRR strategy properties.

Trotwood and West Dayton: Higher-risk, higher-reward territory. Distressed properties are plentiful and cheap, making this a prime zone for wholesalers and experienced flippers who know how to price the risk.
Downtown Dayton and the Oregon District: Emerging markets with growing young professional populations. Short-term rentals and small multifamily properties are gaining traction here.

sections.content: Pro Tip: When evaluating Dayton neighborhoods, always check flood zone maps and local crime statistics before committing. Some areas of West Dayton have high vacancy and blight, which can affect your resale timeline and rental stability. The Montgomery County Auditor's website offers free property data and ownership records that are invaluable for finding distressed sellers.
Types of Real Estate Deals Available in Dayton OH
Wholesale Deals

Dayton is a strong wholesale market because of the sheer volume of distressed and vacant properties scattered throughout the city. Many homeowners are facing probate situations, tax delinquency, or simply inherited properties they don't want to manage. Wholesalers typically lock up these contracts at $20,000 to $50,000 and assign them to cash buyers for $5,000 to $15,000 in assignment fees. If you're new to this strategy, read the Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide to understand the process before you start making offers.
Fix and Flip Opportunities

The fix-and-flip strategy works well in Dayton's mid-tier and upper neighborhoods. A typical flip in Kettering or Oakwood might look like this: purchase at $70,000, invest $40,000 in renovations, and sell for $155,000 to $175,000. That's a gross profit of $45,000 to $65,000 before holding costs and agent fees. The key is accurate rehab estimation and a solid contractor network. Always run the numbers before you commit — plug your deal into the free Deal Calculator at aiwholesail.com to make sure the math works before you sign anything.
Rental and Buy-and-Hold Properties

For long-term investors, Dayton's rental market is compelling. Average rents for a three-bedroom single-family home range from $950 to $1,400 per month depending on the neighborhood. With purchase prices often under $100,000 for decent rental-ready properties, gross rent multipliers and cap rates in Dayton are significantly better than in most major metros. Section 8 housing demand is also high, giving landlords a reliable, government-backed income stream in lower-income areas.
Dayton Real Estate Market Trends to Watch in 2024

items: Rising rents: Dayton rents have increased roughly 8-12% over the past two years, improving cash flow for landlords who purchased at lower price points.
Low inventory: Like most U.S. markets, Dayton is experiencing limited housing inventory, which is pushing retail buyers to bid up prices and creating urgency among investors to find off-market deals.
Continued revitalization: The city has invested heavily in downtown infrastructure, the Oregon District, and the riverfront. These improvements are lifting property values in adjacent neighborhoods.

Investor competition increasing: More out-of-state investors are discovering Dayton. While there's still more opportunity here than in overheated coastal markets, acting quickly on good deals is increasingly important.
Vacancy concerns in certain areas: Parts of North Dayton and some inner-city zip codes still struggle with high vacancy rates. Thorough due diligence remains essential.

How to Find Off-Market Deals in Dayton OH

The most profitable real estate deals in Dayton OH rarely show up on Zillow or the MLS. Off-market properties — those sold directly by motivated sellers before they're publicly listed — give investors the best shot at below-market prices and less competition. Common strategies include direct mail campaigns targeting tax-delinquent owners, driving for dollars to spot vacant properties, building relationships with local probate attorneys, and working with a local real estate wholesaler who already has a pipeline of deals. For a full breakdown of off-market strategies, read How to Find Off-Market Real Estate Deals — it covers the top tactics that work in markets just like Dayton.
Tips for Out-of-State Investors Looking at Dayton

Dayton has attracted a growing number of out-of-state investors, particularly from high-cost markets like California, New York, and the Pacific Northwest. If you're investing remotely, here's how to do it right.

items: Build a local team first: You need a reliable property manager, a general contractor, a real estate attorney familiar with Ohio law, and a local agent who works with investors. Don't buy a single property until this team is in place.

Visit before you commit: At minimum, make one trip to Dayton to walk the neighborhoods, see the properties, and meet your team face to face. What looks good on paper can look very different on the ground.

Use data to vet deals remotely: Platforms like AIWholesail help out-of-state investors quickly analyze deal quality, neighborhood data, and comparable sales without needing to be on the ground for every opportunity. Explore the Dayton market data at aiwholesail.com/markets/dayton-oh.

Understand Ohio landlord-tenant law: Ohio is considered a relatively landlord-friendly state, but eviction timelines and notice requirements still vary by county. Know the rules before you place a tenant.

Start with turnkey or light-value-add properties: For your first Dayton deal, avoid deep rehab projects until you know your contractor can execute. A turnkey or light cosmetic flip is a lower-risk entry point when you're investing from out of state.
Analyze every deal with discipline: Never let low prices make you sloppy. Read How to Analyze Real Estate Deals Like a Pro to make sure you're evaluating all the right numbers before you close.

sections.content: Pro Tip: Montgomery County offers free online access to property ownership records, tax history, and assessed values through the county auditor's website. This is one of the best free tools available for identifying motivated sellers and absentee owners in Dayton — start there before spending money on a paid list service.
Is Dayton OH Right for Your Investment Goals?

Dayton isn't a market for everyone. If you're chasing rapid appreciation or luxury flips, there are better markets. But if you want strong cash flow, affordable entry points, consistent rental demand, and a steady supply of distressed properties to wholesale or flip, Dayton checks a lot of boxes. The fundamentals are sound, the competition is still manageable compared to larger metros, and the barriers to entry are low enough that even newer investors can get started with limited capital. The window of relative undervaluation won't last forever — markets like this tend to attract more attention as word gets out.
